item.title: Why We Splurge on Small Luxuries When Money Is Tight
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Why We Splurge on Small Luxuries When Money Is Tight

Once a recession habit, the small treat is now a way of life.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • During economic downturns, spending on small luxuries rises while spending on larger ones falls.
  • For a generation priced out of the big purchases, the small treat has stopped being temporary.
  • Luxury brands have responded by shrinking products into miniatures that sell the label without the price tag.

We find ourselves in the middle of another financial crisis. Big purchases are out of the question. We only buy the essentials. When did all those artisanal soaps, aromatherapy fragrances, or the extortionately priced speciality iced latte on the way into the office become essential?

Something has happened in the way we view, and buy, luxury goods.

We do not give up luxury. We buy it smaller.

Hard times change how we shop, though not always in the way you would expect. When money gets tight, we start reclassifying what is essential and what is merely nice to have. What we tend not to do, however, is give up luxuries altogether. They too become essential, and we just buy them smaller.

Marketers have named this the small treat economy. Buy a little something from a big-name label, and you get a taste of luxury without the costs that usually come attached. Luxury brands have been quick to respond.

Dior and Hermès have widened their makeup lines. Diptyque sells its candles in miniature, and Coach now offers more small accessories like bag charms and key rings. The balancing act is to sell luxury to cash-strapped customers without letting the brand itself feel cheap.

In doing so, they are appealing to a new kind of shopper. One who has begun to psychologically reclassify what is worth splurging on. Understanding this behaviour takes us back to a department store at the turn of the millennium.

Lauder’s lipstick

By late 2001, the American economy was already contracting. The dot-com bubble had burst in the spring, and the September attacks accelerated an economic decline that was well underway. Leonard Lauder, then chairman of Estée Lauder, braced for the grim financial realities ahead. But he noticed something odd.

While the rest of the department store fell quiet, one counter stayed busy, and one product kept selling: lipstick. This lipstick effect let Lauder argue that sales of small, affordable luxuries could double as an audit on the state of the nation’s finances.

The designer coat or handbag is suddenly out of the question, but a lipstick from that same designer? That still feels affordable, and it still feels like a treat.

From that single observation came one of the stranger ways we have tried to analyse the state of the economy.

Small treats like designer lipstick are common purchases during hard times.
Source: DS stories / Pexels

Shopping in a financial crisis

One of the most detailed audits we have comes from MacDonald and Dildar (2020), who examined household spending during the Great Recession using the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Expenditures Survey. They found a significant rise in average cosmetics spending among younger women in particular, and evidence that the money had been substituted away from clothing. Which is, more or less, exactly what Lauder observed himself.

article continues after advertisement

The rise held regardless of marital or employment status, which went against the original explanations that the literature had previously favoured. Hill and colleagues (2012) had run a series of studies and similarly found that recessionary cues reduced women’s desire for most products but consistently increased their desire for beauty products. However, their interpretation of this behaviour was evolutionary. They argued that hard times heightened mate-attraction motives, which beauty products can help serve.

So we have experiments pointing one way and household spending data pointing another. If the expectation really is mate attraction, single women should be driving the numbers. In the spending data, they are not. Everyone is.

The effect appears to be real, but why it happens is still being argued about. The answer may lie in an analysis of the current economy and who has been hit the hardest.

The lipstick effect is for life, not just for recessions

The old assumption was that once the crisis was over, we would all go back to spending freely, but that has not happened. After years of one crisis running into the next, and prices that only ever seem to go up, the luxury treat has stopped being a one-off for special occasions and turned into a way of life.

Today, much of the world is in some calamity or another, and an entire generation has grown up knowing little else. Their careers began later and on shakier ground. They seek employment in a labour market that has been quietly rethinking how many early-career people it actually needs. Things once widely affordable have become extravagances. The down payment on a first home or buying that diamond ring and marrying your childhood sweetheart; these are goals that drift a little further away each year.

article continues after advertisement

The milestones their parents took as standard have slipped somewhere between the improbable and the imaginary. Batamirova and Thrassou (2025) argue that Gen Z and millennial luxury consumption has reorganised itself around smaller and more attainable purchases, and it is not hard to see why. If the big thing is never going to arrive, why save for it? Repeated small indulgences become a sensible second best.

Nowadays, it is not just lipstick. Look at the recent downturns and the same pattern shows up in other little pleasures. From gourmet food to designer accessories and even curated stationery, a whole category of small luxury consumables has appeared. When the outlook is bleak, and the budget is tight, a small indulgence you can still afford is a practical and reliable way to feel a bit better about yourself and, indeed, the world.

We still want luxury, whatever the economy is doing. That feeling has not changed. But the size of the thing we buy, and how often we buy it, definitely has.

item.title: A Couples Therapist Goes to a Party
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

A Couples Therapist Goes to a Party

Personal Perspective: Four things a party taught me.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • A party is a socially acceptable relational playground full of relational quickies, shallow or deep.
  • When someone swipes away mid-conversation, it's not personal. It's the law of two feet.
  • A party lets you choose which self-state to lead with, and meeting different people expands you.
  • Nobody expects a goodbye round. You can leave things open without shame.
Parties are relational playgrounds.
Source: Shai Shachar

I don't go to parties a lot. I consider myself an extrovert, but as I age, I'm evolving more into an ambivert.

I'm a couples therapist. I spend my days in very intimate conversations with one or two people, between 60 and 120 minutes. We are off our phones. We are 100 percent present. I have the privilege and responsibility of meeting people at their most vulnerable, which is a rare occupation. And I don't just talk with my clients. We work through, laugh, cry, challenge, rupture, repair, and play. Call it emotional and mental intimacy. In that sense, one could consider me a paid intimacy worker. Since I mostly work remotely, every interaction in my day is either super deep or nonexistent, like a server at a store.

Last week my wife and daughter were still at camp, and my son was at a sleepover. There was a party. I said I'd go. Friends drove me so I could have a drink and relax. I got there and realized I was out of my comfort zone. Here are four things I learned that night.

A party is a swingers party

As we previously wrote, there are three channels to connect with another person: physical, mental, and emotional. A good, mind-stretching conversation is mind-mating, or intellectual intercourse. A conversation where you share feelings and feel alive is hearting, or emotional lovemaking.

A party is a socially acceptable event where people go in hopes of mind-mating and hearting with others.

With many people in a room, we tend to have relational quickies. One-minute or five-minute stands, where we both exchange something. It can be shallow, like where I got the sweater. It can be very deep, like my parents got divorced when I was 3; both are allowed within four minutes of meeting a person. They stretch us, because these are people we don't live or work with.

People want this. Some of us do it at work, in the gym, church, or the pool, and some are very good at it. I'm not. My biological clock for a relational encounter is 60 to 120 minutes. I'm not in shape.

People leave in the middle

I was talking with someone about a vision I have for a Netflix special. She was loving it. She was yes-ending me. We were brainstorming over my and my wife's careers. Then somebody said hello to her, and the conversation ended. She turned. That was it.

article continues after advertisement

I was surprised and micro-insulted. What? How could she end now? We just shared a moment.

Then I asked myself why I was getting insulted. In the clinic, I control the setting. I know when the conversation ends. I can choreograph it. At a party, there is the two-feet law. If you're not contributing or gaining anything, you move. It's not personal; it's the convention. And since it's brief, you never know how deep it will go. Sometimes you confess to a stranger what you wouldn't dare tell a close acquaintance. Other times it's about the type of cheese on the table.

You get to choose which you shows up

We all have different parts, or self-states. The confident, silly, flirty, professional, sad parts. In daily life, we lead with two or three relational business cards at home and at work, with people who know us in a certain light. At a party, you get to choose which self-state to lead with. In a five-minute stand, you can stop in the middle and pivot.

Early in the evening, people asked how my summer has been. I automatically stressed the challenges. The adjustment since we moved, the complexities of summer camp. That's where I naturally go. In psychotherapy, we call this negative attention: getting attention through what's not working, difficulties, pain, and the darker shades.

In my third relational quickie, I realized I wanted to change this. I chose honest and positive, without faking happiness. The true truth is that I'm grateful; I'm learning all these things, and I never really realized that. The following encounters focused on learning, expansion, and realizations instead of difficulty. What let me switch was curiosity over certainty, the first equation in the relational math of change.

And it goes past what you choose to bring. Every person in that room is different; they force, entice, and invite other parts of you. You get to discover yourself through the party. That's the genius of it.

I'm used to having deep intimate playdates. A party is one big playground. Parties, like marriage, are a relational gym for all your self-states. What I got to practice that night was the playful, improvisational, positive parts of me.

Nobody's expecting you to say goodbye

My ride was leaving. I started to say goodbye, which can be another long, emotional round with every single person I shared a somewhat meaningful conversation, at least for me.

Then I stopped. How many people do I actually need to say goodbye to? How many conversations passed the bar? I do the closing round because I'm used to closing every conversation with ritualistic awareness and sensitivity. That night I realized I didn't need to. Part of the social contract is that you can leave things open. The only exception is the host. Thank you and goodbye, the minimum to show respect. Everyone else is not expecting it. You get to leave without shame or heaviness.

article continues after advertisement

I came home invigorated and started to process the evening. It was an intense relational workout. It shed light on why I chose my profession, and why people love parties. We are relational creatures who crave connection.

Do I want more relational quickies? How do I create more relational playgrounds in my life? The truth is sometimes you just want to dabble. Sometimes you just want to party.

item.title: What Decides Whether a Day Is Seized?
item.description:
Resilience

What Decides Whether a Day Is Seized?

A dying teacher taught me that carpe diem was never about doing more.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • A day is seized not by what fills it, but by how fully we attend to it.
  • Meaning—a point of light in the darkest moments—can make even a hospice room a place of carpe diem.
  • We remember days by their best moment and their ending, not by their length or busyness.
  • Knowing time is limited doesn't spoil a day; it is often what finally makes us notice it.

Some time ago, a woman in a hospice care unit asked to meet me. We had never met; we had no point of connection I could think of. I felt honored and puzzled in equal measure. (Identifying details have been changed.)

The head nurse told me, before I entered, that the woman had been there for several weeks—without a single visitor or phone call.

Her room was what you would expect: still. No flowers. No cards. She was a retired teacher—almost 40 years in the classroom, thousands of children taught, four of her own raised, a beloved husband gone nearly two decades. Her children were busy, she said, without a trace of bitterness. She did not expect them to come.

The connection turned out to be secondhand. A young physician on her unit had once been my student, and he had mentioned something from class: that the most powerful protection in life against adversity is a point of meaning—something that provides light even in the darkest moments of a person's life. She had asked to meet me for one reason. She wanted to tell me, teacher to teacher, that she agreed. Being a teacher and being a mother, she said, had been hers.

I came for 30 minutes. I left almost four hours later. She was funny—gently, unhurriedly funny—about her own life, in a room most of us would find unbearable. As I stood to say goodbye, planning to ask whether I might visit weekly, I noticed a small sticky note on the closet by her bed. It read: carpe diem.

She noticed that I noticed. As I was leaving, she said, with that same gentle humor, that she was happy to have made my day a carpe diem. We laughed. We said goodbye.

Four days later, I returned to visit her and found her room empty.

The Question Hiding Inside "Seize the Day"

Everyone knows the command: Seize the day. Almost no one asks the follow-up question: What decides whether a day was seized?

The popular answer is volume. A seized day is a full one—adventurous, productive, photographed. By that standard, a woman confined to a hospice bed, with no visitors and no future, could not seize anything. And yet she had the note on her closet, and she meant it, and by any honest accounting, she seized that day more completely than I did most of mine. She also seized a piece of mine—and knew it, and joked about it.

Psychology suggests she understood something the popular reading misses: Days are not made significant by what happens in them. They are made significant by three quieter variables—meaning, attention, and memory.

Meaning Decides First

Viktor Frankl, who observed human endurance in the most extreme conditions imaginable, concluded that those who could connect their suffering to something that mattered—a person, a task, a purpose—withstood what those without such an anchor could not (Frankl, 1959/2006). Decades of research on meaning in life have followed his lead: a sense that one's life has significance and coherence is consistently associated with resilience and better health.

This is what I call a point of meaning—the light source that keeps functioning when everything else goes dark. Notice what her points of meaning were: not achievements pending, but a life already given to children, her own and other people's. Meaning does not require a future. Hers was entirely behind her in one sense, and entirely present in the room in another—because meaning, once made, is portable. It travels into hospice rooms. It survives the absence of visitors.

article continues after advertisement

Attention Decides Second

A day cannot be seized by someone who is not there for it. In a landmark experience-sampling study, Killingsworth and Gilbert (2010) found that people's minds wander during roughly half of their waking moments—and that a wandering mind tends to be an unhappier one, largely regardless of the activity. Much of what we call an unremarkable day is simply an unattended one.

She was the most present person in that building. No phone, no schedule, no elsewhere to be—circumstances forced some of that, certainly. But presence was also her craft; 40 years in a classroom trains a person to be exactly where the moment is. Research on savoring shows that deliberately attending to an experience while it happens amplifies and extends it (Bryant & Veroff, 2007). Four hours passed in her room like 30 minutes. That is what full attention does to time.

Memory Decides Third

Here is the strangest finding of all: A day is not stored as its average. Retrospective evaluations largely neglect duration; we remember an experience by its emotional peak and by how it ended (Fredrickson & Kahneman, 1993). A long, busy, unattended day collapses in memory to almost nothing. A single luminous moment, well ended, becomes the day.

She engineered both, whether she knew the research or not. The peak was the meeting itself—two strangers discovering they were colleagues in the oldest profession of caring for other people's growth. And the ending was perfect: her joke, our laughter, the goodbye. She built me a memory to specification. It is the reason I can still see the sticky note.

The Empty Room

There is one more variable, and it is the hardest one: knowing the days are numbered.

We tend to assume that awareness of endings poisons the present. The evidence points the other way. When people are prompted to notice that a good chapter is ending soon, they engage more, savor more, and extract more happiness from the time that remains (Kurtz, 2008). Scarcity does not spoil the day. Scarcity is frequently what finally makes us show up for it.

She lived at the far end of that truth. Her days were visibly few, and rather than emptying them, the fact concentrated them. The sticky note was not decoration. It was method.

I had planned to visit her once or twice a week. I did not get one more visit. I am left instead with what she gave me in a single afternoon, which turns out to be the answer to the question in the title. What decides whether a day is seized? Not its contents, but instead, three things she had in abundance and most of us keep postponing: something that means enough to light the dark, full attention to the moment you are actually in, and one good moment—well ended, preferably with laughter—for memory to keep.

article continues after advertisement

By that standard, any day qualifies. Even a Tuesday. Even a hospice room.

Especially a hospice room.

item.title: Why Smart People Make Foolish Romantic Decisions
item.description:
Relationships

Why Smart People Make Foolish Romantic Decisions

The gap between what we know and what we do in love.

Posted August 1, 2026

Key points
  • Some of the brightest people repeatedly make poor romantic choices.
  • Smart people excel primarily at deliberative thinking, whereas wise people rely more on intuitive reasoning.
  • Healthy relationships require more than intelligence; they require the integration of thought and feeling.
  • Romantic flourishing depends on wisdom: the ability to discern what truly matters in love.

"Be as smart as you can, but remember that it is always better to be wise than to be smart." —Alan Alda

"A wise girl knows her limits; a smart girl knows that she has none." —Marilyn Monroe

Being smart is widely regarded as a valuable cognitive asset. It enables people to acquire knowledge quickly, solve complex problems, and succeed in demanding careers. Yet intellectual brilliance offers no guarantee of romantic success. Some of the brightest people repeatedly choose unsuitable partners, ignore obvious warning signs, or try to solve emotional problems with logic alone.

Why does this happen? The answer lies in the distinction between being smart and being wise—and in recognizing that successful romantic relationships demand more than intelligence.

Types of Cognition

Source: Tiger Lily/Pexels

Following Spinoza's (1677) lead, we can distinguish three major forms of cognition: emotional intuition, deliberative thinking, and intuitive reasoning.

Emotional intuition operates rapidly and automatically, generating immediate feelings of attraction, fear, or affection. Deliberative thinking is slower and more analytical, allowing us to compare alternatives, weigh evidence, and solve explicit problems.

A third form—intuitive reasoning, a hallmark of wisdom—goes beyond both. Rather than opposing emotion and reason, it integrates them. It combines experience, emotional sensitivity, long-term perspective, and practical judgment into an immediate yet well-calibrated understanding. Expert decision-making often relies on this kind of intuitive reasoning. Likewise, enduring love depends on romantic resonance—a spontaneous yet deeply informed responsiveness to one's partner. Indeed, spouses' automatic attitudes toward one another, rather than their consciously reported attitudes, predict future marital satisfaction. Couples with more positive implicit attitudes are less likely to experience declines in relationship quality. These spontaneous responses bypass self-presentational biases and often become self-fulfilling prophecies in intimate relationships (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

From this perspective, smart people primarily excel at deliberative thinking, whereas wise people rely more heavily on intuitive reasoning, integrating intellect with emotional understanding. Wisdom resembles expertise: It reflects not merely knowing more but discerning what matters most. Intelligence helps people solve romantic problems; wisdom helps them avoid creating the wrong ones.

article continues after advertisement

The Cognitive Demands of Love

All three forms of cognition contribute to romantic life. Emotional intuition is especially important during the early stages of falling in love, when attraction and emotional resonance create the initial bond. As relationships mature, deliberative thinking becomes valuable for resolving practical problems, coordinating daily life, and making important joint decisions.

Yet flourishing long-term relationships require something more than either passion or analytical skill. They require wisdom. Wisdom enables people to recognize patterns rather than isolated incidents, appreciate character rather than surface traits, balance immediate emotions against long-term consequences, and realize that preserving the relationship often matters more than winning a particular argument. Wisdom begins with recognizing the limits of one's own knowledge—a kind of intellectual humility.

Relationship experts, therefore, often advise us to strive not merely to be right but to be wise. Being right may satisfy the ego; being wise strengthens the relationship.

Common Romantic Mistakes Smart People Make

"An intellectual is a person who's found one thing that's more interesting than sex." —Aldous Huxley

Highly intelligent people often stumble in love not because they lack cognitive ability, but because they overestimate the power of analysis in a domain that also requires emotional wisdom. Common mistakes include:

  • Over-intellectualizing partner choice. Giving excessive weight to education, intelligence, status, or shared interests while undervaluing kindness, generosity, emotional stability, and character.
  • Believing they can change a partner. Smart people often trust the power of persuasion and rational argument, overlooking the fact that lasting personal change occurs more readily through emotional safety and mutual acceptance than through logical debate.
  • Searching for the perfect partner rather than the most suitable one. Intelligence can fuel relentless optimization, encourage endless comparison, and make commitment more difficult.
  • Confusing attraction with compatibility. Intellectual confidence may lead people to believe they can predict a relationship's future after a brief period of intense attraction while overlooking incompatibilities that become apparent only with time.
article continues after advertisement

Wise people, by contrast, know when to apologize instead of insisting on being right, when silence is preferable to argument, why kindness outweighs brilliance in a lifelong partner, and why accepting imperfections is often wiser than endlessly optimizing.

These examples illustrate a broader principle: Intelligence excels at solving problems, whereas wisdom excels at recognizing which problems are worth solving.

Concluding Thoughts

"You can tell whether a man is clever by his answers. You can tell whether a man is wise by his questions." — Naguib Mahfouz

There are many paths to enduring love. Intelligence undoubtedly helps people understand relationships, communicate effectively, and solve practical problems. Yet intelligence alone is not enough. Romantic flourishing depends on wisdom—the capacity to integrate thought with feeling, immediate desires with long-term values, and one's own perspective with that of one's partner.

The distinction between being smart and being wise is not absolute but gradual. The good news is that wisdom can be cultivated through experience, humility, and emotional openness. Intelligence becomes a far greater asset when guided by wisdom. Smart people know many things. Wise people know what truly matters. In love, that difference often determines whether a relationship merely survives—or genuinely flourishes.
